Anacardium occidentale.evidence: The seed is surrounded by a double-shell that contains an allergenic phenolic resin, anacardic acid - which is a a potent skin irritant chemically related to the better-known and also toxic allergenic oil urushiol, which is found in the related poison ivy and lacquer tree.
Anacardium occidentale.line: It can cause an itchy skin rash.

Anemonastrum canadense.evidence: It is likely that most anemones contain similar caustic irritants to other members of the family Ranunculaceae.
Anemonastrum canadense.line: It might have sap that irritates the skin.

Anthemis cotula.evidence: The foliage may also cause skin irritation.
Anthemis cotula.line: The leaves can irritate the skin.

Apocynum cannabinum.evidence: The stems contain a white sap capable of causing skin blisters.
Apocynum cannabinum.line: The sap can cause skin blisters.

Araujia sericifera.evidence: Skin contact with its sap can cause rashes.
Araujia sericifera.line: Its sap can cause rashes on skin.

Arctium lappa.evidence: The minute, sharply-pointed, bristly pappus hairs easily detach from the top of the achenes and are carried by the slightest breeze – attaching to skin, mucous membranes, and eyes where they can cause severe dermal irritation, possible respiratory manifestations, and ophthalmia.
Arctium lappa.line: Small hairs can irritate skin and eyes.

Armoracia rusticana.evidence: When cut or grated, enzymes from within the plant cells digest sinigrin (a glucosinolate) to produce allyl isothiocyanate (mustard oil), which irritates the mucous membranes of the sinuses and eyes.

Arnica montana.evidence: Contact with the plant can also cause skin irritation.

Arum italicum.evidence: Additionally, the sap of the plant can cause skin irritation, so it is recommended that gloves should be worn when removing it from an area.

Arum maculatum.evidence: They contain oxalates of saponins, which have needle-shaped crystals that irritate the skin, mouth, tongue, and throat, and result in swelling of throat, difficulty breathing, burning pain, and upset stomach.
Arum maculatum.line: Tiny crystals can irritate the skin and cause burning pain.

Asparagus aethiopicus.evidence: aethiopicus can cause gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea, vomiting and abdominal pain, and contact with the skin may cause dermatitis.
Asparagus aethiopicus.line: Contacting it can cause skin irritation.

Calotropis gigantea.evidence: The milky latex sap of Calotropis gigantea is a known cause of toxic keratoconjunctivitis and reversible vision loss.
Calotropis gigantea.line: Its sap can cause eye injury and vision loss.

Caltha palustris.evidence: Contact of the skin or mucous membranes with the juices can cause blistering or inflammation, and gastric illness if ingested.
Caltha palustris.line: Juices can cause skin to blister or inflame.

Centella asiatica.evidence: Contact dermatitis and skin irritation can result from topical application.

Clematis drummondii.evidence: The sap of this plant is caustic, although its foliage, stems, and roots can be used for dye if caution is used while handling and if breathing the fumes is avoided.

Clematis ligusticifolia.evidence: Like the rest of the genus Clematis, it contains essential oils and compounds which are extremely irritating to the skin and mucous membranes.
Clematis ligusticifolia.line: It can be very irritating to the skin.

Clematis paniculata.evidence: They would use the leaves to produce blisters as a counter-irritant and the sap to help heal wounds.

Cneoridium dumosum.evidence: Despite attractive qualities like its distinctive fragrance and flowers, this species may cause blistering and burning rashes to people after contact with its foliage, a phenomenon common with members of the citrus family, known as phytophotodermatitis.
Cneoridium dumosum.line: Its leaves can cause burning or blistering rashes.

Cnidoscolus stimulosus.evidence: As the common names imply, the urticating hairs on this plant contain a caustic irritant that inflicts a painful sting to those who contact it with bare skin.
Cnidoscolus stimulosus.line: Hairs on it cause a painful sting to skin.

Cnidoscolus texanus.evidence: Contact with the plant, even the inadvertent, gentle brushing of exposed skin in passing, results in intense pain, including a burning, stinging, itching rash lasting for hours, with the fine hairs breaking off in the skin secreting caustic irritants, which are highly acidic in pH.
Cnidoscolus texanus.line: Its hairs cause skin to sting, burn, and itch.

Codiaeum variegatum.evidence: Complications stemming from sap contact may range from mild to extreme burning pain, itchiness, rash or temporary dulling of the senses; depending on the region of the body affected, this sensory reaction may include temporary or long-term complications with sight, hearing, taste, feeling or smell, among other issues.
Codiaeum variegatum.line: The sap can cause burning pain and a rash.

Conium maculatum.evidence: Contact of the leaves with bare skin can result in rash and persistent blisters through phototoxicity, the sensitisation of the skin to sunlight.
Conium maculatum.line: The leaves can cause skin blisters in sunlight.

Crassula ovata.evidence: Exposure to sap or leaves can cause dermatitis in humans.
Crassula ovata.line: Sap or leaves can cause skin irritation.

Crinum asiaticum.evidence: Some reports indicate exposure to the sap may cause skin irritation.

Cucurbita foetidissima.evidence: However, prolonged contact can cause skin irritation.
Cucurbita foetidissima.line: Staying in contact can irritate skin.

Cynanchum laeve.evidence: Its sap can cause eye irritation damaging mucous membranes.
Cynanchum laeve.line: The sap can hurt your eyes.

Cypripedium reginae.evidence: The foliage hairs may cause a rash similar to the one caused by poison ivy.
Cypripedium reginae.line: Its hairs can cause a rash.

Daphne gnidium.evidence: Skin contact with the sap can cause dermatitis The chance of death is small yet possible within 6 hours after direct consumption.

Daphne laureola.evidence: Hand-pulling is effective against small infestations (gloves must be worn to protect against the caustic sap); shrubs too large or too small to pull must be dug out.
Daphne laureola.line: The sap can cause skin rashes.

Daucus carota.evidence: Like many other species of Apiaceae, the leaves of the wild carrot may cause phytophotodermatitis; skin contact with the foliage, especially wet foliage, can cause skin irritation in some people, so caution should be used when handling the plant.
Daucus carota.line: Leaves can cause skin irritation in sunlight.

Dioscorea communis.evidence: It has been suggested that black bryony be used topically with caution, due to a tendency for the plant to cause painful blisters.
Dioscorea communis.line: It can cause painful blisters on the skin.

Dirca palustris.evidence: The plant is known to be an emetic, laxative, and vesicant with some people developing severe skin irritation upon contact with the bark.

Echium plantagineum.evidence: Paterson's curse can kill horses, and irritate the udders of dairy cows and the skin of humans.

Epipremnum aureum.evidence: Excessive contact with the plant can also lead to general skin irritation or contact dermatitis.

Eucnide urens.evidence: 5 cm long with stinging hairs which are also found on the stems and buds.
Eucnide urens.line: It has hairs that sting the skin.

Euphorbia amygdaloides.evidence: The milky latex of the plant is toxic and can cause irritation on contact with the skin.
Euphorbia amygdaloides.line: Its milky sap can irritate skin.

Euphorbia bicolor.evidence: The white sap characteristic of this family can cause irritation to the skin or eyes of people who are exposed to it.
Euphorbia bicolor.line: The white sap can irritate skin or eyes.

Euphorbia cyparissias.evidence: Contact with the sap can cause skin reactions.
Euphorbia cyparissias.line: The sap can cause skin reactions.

Euphorbia hypericifolia.evidence: It normally grows up to in height, and contains milky sap which can cause skin and eye irritation.
Euphorbia hypericifolia.line: Its milky sap can irritate skin and eyes.

Euphorbia lathyris.evidence: Handling may cause skin irritation as the plant produces latex.
Euphorbia lathyris.line: Its latex can irritate the skin.

Euphorbia myrsinites.evidence: The plant's milky sap can cause significant skin and eye irritation in humans and may cause blindness with contact with the eyes.
Euphorbia myrsinites.line: Its milky sap can irritate skin and eyes.

Euphorbia ophthalmica.evidence: " However, this advice is dangerous since the white sap of many Euphorbia species is extremely irritating to the skin and eyes.
Euphorbia ophthalmica.line: The white sap irritates the skin and eyes.

Euphorbia peplus.evidence: The plant's sap is toxic to rapidly replicating human tissue, and has long been used as a traditional remedy for common skin lesions.
Euphorbia peplus.line: The sap can damage human skin tissue.

Euphorbia terracina.evidence: As with many other Euphorbia species, exposure to its milky sap may cause irritation to skin, eyes, and digestive tracts.
Euphorbia terracina.line: Its milky sap can irritate skin and eyes.

Ficaria verna.evidence: Contact with damaged or crushed Ficaria leaves can cause itching, rashes or blistering on the skin or mucosa.
Ficaria verna.line: Crushed leaves can cause skin rashes or blisters.

Ficus carica.line: The sap can cause skin reactions in sunlight.

Ficus pumila.evidence: Like other plant species in the family Moraceae, contact with the milky sap of Ficus pumila can cause phytophotodermatitis, a potentially serious skin inflammation.
Ficus pumila.line: Its sap can cause serious skin inflammation.

Fumaria officinalis.evidence: and two thousand years ago, Dioscorides wrote in () and Pliny the Elder in that rubbing the eyes with the sap or latex of the plant causes tears, like acrid smoke () does to the eyes.
Fumaria officinalis.line: Its sap can make eyes water.

Heracleum mantegazzianum.evidence: The sap of giant hogweed is phototoxic and causes phytophotodermatitis in humans, resulting in blisters and scarring.
Heracleum mantegazzianum.line: The sap can cause blisters and scarring.

Heracleum maximum.evidence: Because of this, phytophotodermatitis causing skin blistering may occur after coming into contact with the sap on a sunny day.
Heracleum maximum.line: Its sap can cause blisters in the sun.

Heracleum sosnowskyi.evidence: It is dangerous for humans because even small drops of the plant's sap can cause skin photosensitivity and burns.
Heracleum sosnowskyi.line: Sap can cause skin burns in sunlight.

Heracleum sphondylium.evidence: It contains some of the same phytophototoxic compounds (furanocoumarins), albeit at much lower concentrations, and there is evidence that the sap from common hogweed can also produce phytophotodermatitis (burns and rashes) in sensitive individuals when contaminated skin is exposed to sunlight.

Hypericum androsaemum.evidence: androsaemum does not contain hypericin, a chemical present in other Hypericum species that can cause skin irritation and other undesirable side effects, the plant is more widely used in topical applications and skincare.

Hypericum punctatum.evidence: Though insects eat the plant, foraging mammals seldom feed on the foliage as leaves contain hypericin which, in mammals, can blister skin and irritate the digestive tract.

Iris cristata.evidence: Handling the plant may cause a skin irritation or an allergic reaction, and there is also a risk of dermatitis.

Iris lacustris.evidence: Handling the plant may also cause a skin irritation or an allergic reaction.

Iris sibirica.evidence: Also handling the plant may cause a skin irritation or an allergic reaction.

Laportea canadensis.evidence: When the stinging nettles come in contact with the skin, the unlucky individual is dealt a painful burning stinging sensation, sometimes with barbs left in the skin.
Laportea canadensis.line: It can cause a painful burning sensation on the skin.

Lupinus hirsutissimus.evidence: The stem and herbage are coated in long, stiff hairs that sting skin when touched.

Mangifera indica.evidence: Allergenic urushiols are present in the fruit peel.
Mangifera indica.line: The peel has oils that cause skin rashes.

Marah fabacea.evidence: The liquid inside the fruit is an eye irritant, and the spines on the fruit are irritating to the skin.
Marah fabacea.line: Liquid inside can irritate eyes and skin.

Moneses uniflora.evidence: The Kwakwaka'wakw people have used Moneses uniflora in poultices for swelling and pain, as it causes blisters.
Moneses uniflora.line: It can cause blisters on the skin.

Monstera deliciosa.evidence: The unripe green fruits can irritate the throat and the latex of the leaves and vines can create rashes in the skin, because both contain calcium oxalate: that is the reason why the fruits have to be consumed when the scales lift up.
Monstera deliciosa.line: The sap can create rashes on the skin.

Nerium oleander.evidence: Prolonged contact with sap may cause skin irritation, eye inflammation and dermatitis.
Nerium oleander.line: Its sap can irritate skin and eyes.

Nolina texana.evidence: Nolina texana is reported to cause sunburn (phototoxicity) by elevating blood phylloerythrin levels in association with liver problems.
Nolina texana.line: It can cause sunburn on the skin.

Oenothera glazioviana.evidence: It is roughly hairy in texture, the hairs with reddish blistering or glandular bases.

Opuntia microdasys.evidence: If not removed they will cause considerable skin irritation so the plants must be treated with caution.

Ornithogalum umbellatum.evidence: Prolonged contact may lead to skin irritation.
Ornithogalum umbellatum.line: Long contact can irritate the skin.

Parthenocissus inserta.evidence: the fruit and leaves contain needle-shaped crystals of calcium oxalate monohydrate called raphide, which may cause blistering or rashes if touched or consumed.
Parthenocissus inserta.line: The leaves and fruit can cause skin blisters or rashes.

Pastinaca sativa.evidence: The shoots and leaves of parsnip must be handled with care, as its sap contains furanocoumarins, phototoxic chemicals that cause blisters on the skin when it is exposed to sunlight, a condition known as phytophotodermatitis.
Pastinaca sativa.line: Sap causes skin blisters in the sunlight.

Pentaglottis sempervirens.evidence: Both the leaves and stem can cause skin irritation.
Pentaglottis sempervirens.line: The leaves and stem can irritate skin.

Persicaria hydropiper.evidence: Wild water pepper produces oils that cause skin irritation.

Phacelia campanularia.evidence: The juice, sap, or hairs may cause irritation or a skin rash and should be washed from skin as soon as possible.
Phacelia campanularia.line: The juice or hairs can irritate the skin.

Phacelia sericea.evidence: It should be handled with care as the long flower hairs have been reported to irritate skin.

Plumeria rubra.evidence: The branches are somewhat brittle and when broken, ooze a white latex that can be irritating to the skin and mucous membranes.
Plumeria rubra.line: Its white sap can irritate the skin.

Pulsatilla occidentalis.evidence: Western pasqueflower likely contains ranunculin and protoanemonin, an irritant glycoside and its aglycone, as these are seen in most members of this genus and the plant's latex is irritating.
Pulsatilla occidentalis.line: Its sap can irritate the skin.

Ranunculus abortivus.evidence: As in other buttercups, the leaves are mildly toxic, containing a blistering agent, but they are eaten by cottontail rabbits.
Ranunculus abortivus.line: The leaves can cause skin to blister.

Ranunculus hispidus.evidence: All parts of the plant are mildly toxic if eaten and could cause minor skin irritation if touched.
Ranunculus hispidus.line: It can cause minor skin irritation.

Ranunculus repens.evidence: Treatments were limited to topical use as the sap of fresh buttercups contains irritant compounds that can cause dermatitis and blistering.
Ranunculus repens.line: The sap can cause skin blistering.

Ranunculus sceleratus.evidence: When the leaves are wrinkled, damaged or crushed, they bring out unsightly sores and blisters on human skin.
Ranunculus sceleratus.line: Crushed leaves can cause sores and blisters on skin.

Rhus integrifolia.evidence: Allergic reactions may also result from skin contact with sap from some of the genera.

Rhus ovata.evidence: There are unconfirmed reports that Rhus ovata contains urushiol, the chemical irritant in plants such as poison ivy.

Ricinus communis.evidence: The sap of the plant causes skin rashes.
Ricinus communis.line: The sap can cause skin rashes.

Scaevola taccada.evidence: Drops from the plant were used in cases of eye irritation by Chamorro breath-hold spearfishermen in the Mariana Islands.

Schinus terebinthifolia.evidence: Contact with the “sap” from a cut or bruised tree can result in rash, lesions, oozing sores, severe itching, welts, and reddening and swelling (especially of the eyes).
Schinus terebinthifolia.line: The sap can cause rashes, sores, and swelling in the eyes.

Sedum acre.evidence: The leaves contain an acrid fluid that can cause skin rashes.
Sedum acre.line: The leaves have fluid that can cause skin rashes.

Solanum mauritianum.evidence: The dust-like fine hairs from the plant can cause irritation to the throat, nose, eyes and skin.
Solanum mauritianum.line: Fine hairs can irritate the skin and eyes.

Symplocarpus foetidus.evidence: While high quantities of the root can produce nausea and vomiting, headaches, and dizziness, handling the fresh leaves can burn skin.

Syngonium podophyllum.evidence: It is not unusual to find these growing in Sub-tropical Florida landscapes, where homeowners and Gardeners need to be aware of the severe skin burning sensations caused by the plants sap containing oxalic acid and the eye damage potential from raphides.
Syngonium podophyllum.line: Sap can burn skin and damage eyes.

Toxicodendron diversilobum.evidence: Toxicodendron diversilobum leaves and twigs have a surface oil, urushiol, which causes an allergic reaction.
Toxicodendron diversilobum.line: The oil causes an itchy skin rash.

Toxicodendron pubescens.evidence: All parts of this plant contain urushiol, which can cause severe dermatitis in sensitive individuals.
Toxicodendron pubescens.line: It can cause itchy, blistered skin.

Toxicodendron radicans.evidence: As a poison ivy, it causes urushiol-induced contact dermatitis in most people who touch it, producing an itchy, irritating, and sometimes painful rash.
Toxicodendron radicans.line: Its oil causes an itchy and painful rash.

Toxicodendron rydbergii.evidence: Because it contains urushiol, contact with the plant can cause severe contact dermatitis in most individuals.
Toxicodendron rydbergii.line: It can cause a bad skin rash.

Toxicodendron vernix.evidence: The fruit and leaves of the poison sumac plant contain urushiol, an oil that causes an allergic rash upon contact with skin.
Toxicodendron vernix.line: Its oil causes a rash on the skin.

Trachelospermum jasminoides.evidence: If cut, like most Apocynaceae, they exude a white latex, resembling sticky milk.

Tradescantia virginiana.evidence: Handling the leaves or sap of this plant can cause contact dermatitis leaving skin irritation, redness, and itching in both humans and dogs/cats.
Tradescantia virginiana.line: The sap can make skin red and itchy.

Tradescantia zebrina.evidence: Skin irritation may result from repeated contact with or prolonged handling of the plant—particularly from the clear, watery sap (a characteristic unique to T.
Tradescantia zebrina.line: The clear sap can irritate skin.

Trifolium hybridum.evidence: The plant can irritate skin if handled.

Turricula parryi.evidence: Like many species in the forget-me-not family, poodle-dog bush causes severe irritation if touched, akin to poison oak.
Turricula parryi.line: It causes severe skin irritation when touched.

Urtica chamaedryoides.evidence: Like other nettles, Urtica chamaedryoides produces stinging hairs that cause an insect-venom like sting when touched.
Urtica chamaedryoides.line: It has hairs that sting the skin.

Urtica dioica.evidence: The species is divided into six subspecies, five of which have many hollow stinging hairs called trichomes on the leaves and stems, which act like hypodermic needles, injecting histamine and other chemicals that produce a stinging sensation upon contact ("contact urticaria", a form of contact dermatitis).
Urtica dioica.line: It has hairs that sting the skin.

Urtica ferox.evidence: Its trichomes can cause painful stings, with effects that can last several days or weeks; the sting is strong enough to kill cattle, dogs, and horses.
Urtica ferox.line: Hairs cause painful stings that last for many days.

Urtica urens.evidence: The lower leaves are shorter than their longer petioles and have stinging hairs only.
Urtica urens.line: It has hairs that sting the skin.

Verbascum thapsus.evidence: Animals rarely graze it because of its irritating hairs, and liquid herbicides require surfactants to be effective, as the hair causes water to roll off the plant, much like the lotus effect.
Verbascum thapsus.line: Its hairs can irritate the skin.

Vitis mustangensis.evidence: The fruit can be potentially irritating to the skin when handled, and are mildly unpleasant to eat raw because of bitterness and a high acidity content, however consuming the sweet inner flesh apart from the skins is common.

Wigandia urens.evidence: It is an erect shrubby plant up to 6 meters tall that can develop trichomes and urticating hairs with petioles 2.
Wigandia urens.line: It has hairs that sting the skin.

Zizia aurea.evidence: Care should be taken to thoroughly wash skin exposed to the sap of broken plant tissues, as subsequent exposure to the UV in sunlight may cause burns and blistering - as in the case of several species of the related Apiaceous genus Heracleum - notably H. aurea responsible for the phototoxicity of this species is the furanocoumarin xanthotoxin, a.
Zizia aurea.line: Sap can cause skin burns and blisters in sunlight.
